summary: This standards-track memo defines a URI scheme for the Simple Network Management Protocol. It lets non-SNMP tools refer to SNMP resources, including specific MIB object instances, in a standard form.

eli5.summary: A web link points to a page. This document defines a link style that points to a device's SNMP data.

subtitle: A snmp:// link format that names an SNMP agent, a context and even specific MIB objects.

tldr.problem: Non-SNMP tools and configuration files had no uniform text string to say how to reach a device's SNMP management service or which MIB object instances to read.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4088 defines the snmp URI scheme: an authority (optional securityName, host, optional port), an optional context and an optional OID or OID group with a suffix that picks exact, next or all-under-prefix instances.
tldr.outcome: A URI never carries secrets or keys, so those must be provisioned to the SNMP manager separately.

today: RFC 4088 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2005. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says IANA registered the scheme using the template in its Appendix A.

sections.title: Why SNMP Needs a URI Scheme
sections.content:
SNMP was devised to manage IP devices in-band, over the same interfaces that carry their traffic. It has since been used for devices without in-band IP access, such as Fibre Channel devices, which often use a separate out-of-band IP interface for management.

URIs offer a convenient way to locate that interface and name the protocol. One scenario the RFC gives is an in-band query that returns a URI saying how the device is managed. The new scheme can designate an SNMP context and can also refer to specific object instances within an SNMP MIB.
sections.eli5: If a machine has a special back door for repairs, a link can tell you exactly where the door is and how to knock.

sections.title: Two Ways to Use an SNMP URI
sections.content:
The RFC names two major usage classes. In configuration, the URI is part of how an application holding an SNMP manager is set up; it can come from a configuration file or from a managed device. The data flows between manager and agent but not beyond the manager.

In gateway use, a client sends an SNMP URI to an SNMP gateway, whose manager performs the SNMP requests and returns the information to the client.

In both cases, extra configuration such as a security secret or key should come through some other interface. A device that provides an SNMP URI in an unprotected way should not also provide the secret needed to use it.
sections.eli5: Either a program uses the link itself to ask a device a question, or it hands the link to a helper who asks on its behalf. The password never travels inside the link.

sections.title: Syntax of an SNMP URI
sections.content:
The syntax is given in ABNF. An SNMP URI starts with snmp://, then an authority, then an optional /contextName with an optional ;contextEngineID, then an optional / followed by an OID or a parenthesized OID group and an optional suffix of + or .*.

The userinfo part of the authority, when present, MUST be an SNMP securityName. Passwords or keys must not be placed in the URI. If the port is missing, port 161 is assumed. If the context name is missing, the zero-length string, the default SNMP context, is assumed. The contextEngineID is written as hexadecimal digits and SHOULD be present if more than one context engine at that host and port supports the context.

The encoding rules of RFC 3986 MUST be used, and all multi-byte UTF-8 characters MUST be percent encoded. A URI MUST NOT end with the / that introduces an OID, because an empty string is not a valid OID. A default context can produce a second //, as in snmp://host//oid, which is legal. For that reason, relative references that start with // but have no authority MUST NOT be used; prefixing . or .. avoids the problem.
sections.eli5: The link has slots in a fixed order: who to ask, which collection to look in, and which item you want. Empty slots get sensible defaults.

sections.title: Meaning of Service and Object URIs
sections.content:
A URI with no OIDs is an SNMP service URI: it names a communication endpoint and context rather than a data object. A URI with one or more OIDs is an SNMP object URI. The service part is processed first to find the context, then the OID or OID group is used to generate SNMP operations.

For a single OID there are three formats. No suffix designates the instance named by the OID, and a Get operation is used. A + suffix designates the lexically next instance, using GetNext. A .* suffix designates all instances for which the OID is a strict lexical prefix, found by repeating GetNext until the results leave the prefix or reach endOfMibView. These are listed from most to least precise, and multiple distinct URIs SHOULD NOT be used for the same instance.

An OID group is a parenthesized, comma-separated list. Its members SHOULD be read in a single SNMP operation so that related values, such as an InetAddress and its InetAddressType, are consistent. An object URI MAY also name instances to be written, which causes an SNMP Set, but then the + and .* suffixes MUST NOT be used and the values to write are not part of the URI. Notifications such as traps and informs cannot be generated directly from a URI.
sections.eli5: You can ask for exactly one readout, the one after it, or everything filed under a heading. You can also ask for several readouts together so they match.

sections.title: Transports and SNMP Versions
sections.content:
The snmp scheme is transport independent. UDP is the default transport for backward compatibility, and others may be used, such as SNMP over TCP (RFC 3430). The result of accessing a URI SHOULD NOT depend on which transport is used.

A URI designates SNMPv3, but older versions MAY be used when unavoidable. For SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c, the securityName, contextName and contextEngineID are mapped to and from the community name as described in RFC 3584. If the community name is kept secret, no URI component should reveal significant information about it. The version number is deliberately left out of the scheme, which leaves room for older versions and any future successor to SNMPv3.
sections.eli5: The link does not say which road or which version of the language to use, so it keeps working if those change.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives several examples. snmp://example.com is the default context at port 161. snmp://tester5@example.com:8161 adds the securityName tester5 and port 8161. snmp://example.com/bridge1 names the bridge1 context, and adding ;800002b804616263 picks one context engine.

Three forms, snmp://example.com//1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0, one ending in + and one ending in .*, all designate sysUpTime.0. They are for illustration only, since distinct URIs for the same instance SHOULD NOT be used. The last example, snmp://example.com//(1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7,1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8).*, designates all (ifAdminStatus, ifOperStatus) pairs in the IF-MIB.
sections.eli5: Here are a few sample links, from the simplest one that just names a machine to ones that ask for a pair of readouts for every network port.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Location information about management access may itself be sensitive. A URI cannot encode security models, security levels or credentials, so these must be provided by other means, for example pre-configuring the manager. A securityName in a URI does not by itself authorize its use: the manager SHOULD match it to a securityName it was configured to use, and SHOULD NOT generate operations if it was not.

Gateways carry extra duties. They SHOULD authenticate each client and check its authorization to use a securityName. A gateway without such controls MUST NOT automatically obtain or use authentication material for arbitrary securityNames. It SHOULD protect client communication at least at the SNMP securityLevel used, and SHOULD use encryption if the client supplies a key or secret. As with other SNMP documents, the RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with its cryptographic mechanisms and says deploying versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: A link is just directions, not a key. A helper must check who is asking before using anyone's key for them.

messages.label: SNMP URI
messages.note: The client asks for management information.

viz.caption: ABNF FOR AN SNMP URI (RFC 4088, Section 3)

data.title: snmp-uri syntax
data.code:
snmp-uri        = "snmp://" snmp-authority [ context [ oids ]]

snmp-authority  = [ securityName "@" ] host [ ":" port ]
securityName    = userinfo    ; SNMP securityName

context         = "/" contextName [ ";" contextEngineID ]
contextName     = segment     ; SNMP contextName
contextEngineID = 1*(HEXDIG HEXDIG)    ; SNMP contextEngineID

oids            = "/" ( oid / oid-group ) [ suffix ]
oid-group       = "(" oid *( "," oid ) ")"
oid             = < as specified by [RFC 3061] >
suffix          = "+" / ".*"

viz.caption: OID SUFFIXES AND THE SNMP OPERATIONS BEHIND THEM

items.label: Exact instance
items.desc: Designates the instance named by the OID; read with Get.

items.label: Next instance
items.desc: Designates the lexically next instance; read with GetNext.

items.label: All under prefix
items.desc: Designates instances with the OID as strict prefix; read by repeated GetNext.
